title_en: Shi, Zhang, Gui v. Xu — dispute over portrait rights, reputation rights, and privacy rights
ruling_gist_en: To protect the interests of minors and to expose possible criminal conduct, the poster published information about a minor being harmed on their Weibo account. If the content of the posted Weibo is substantially consistent with objective facts, it complies with the principle of public interest and the principle of the best interests of the child. Such online reporting conduct does not constitute infringement.

full_text_en:
Shi, Zhang, and Gui v. Xu — dispute over portrait rights, reputation rights, and privacy rights

Ruling Summary

To protect the interests of a minor and to expose possible criminal conduct, a person who posts information about harm suffered by a minor on a microblog, where the content of the microblog is substantially consistent with the objective facts, is in compliance with the principle of social public interest and the principle of the best interests of the child. Such online reporting does not constitute infringement.

Plaintiff: Shi, male, 10 years old, Han ethnicity, currently residing in Lai'an County, Anhui Province.

Temporary guardian: Zhang (the biological mother of Shi), 48 years old, residing in Lai'an County, Anhui Province.

Temporary guardian: Gui (the biological father of Shi), 46 years old, residing in Lai'an County, Anhui Province.

Plaintiff: Zhang, female, 48 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Lai'an County, Anhui Province.

Plaintiff: Gui, male, 46 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Lai'an County, Anhui Province.

Defendant: Xu, male, 28 years old, Han ethnicity, residing in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province.

Plaintiffs Shi, Zhang, and Gui filed a lawsuit with the Jiangning District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, against Defendant Xu for a dispute over portrait rights, reputation rights, and privacy rights.

Plaintiffs Shi, Zhang, and Gui alleged: On April 3, 2015, at 21:15, Defendant Xu posted the following content (accompanied by nine photographs) on his Sina Weibo account (username “朝廷半日闲”): “The parents are from a certain district in Nanjing. The boy was lawfully adopted at age 6. The abusive conduct was discovered by the school last year. Recently, the homeroom teacher found that the injuries were becoming increasingly severe, and the child's personality had also changed significantly, showing psychological behavior such as fear of crowds. After multiple efforts by the homeroom teacher and subject teachers to no avail, they sought help online. We earnestly request the assistance of the media and everyone. We hope that through our help, this child can escape his current predicament.” At 22:40 on the same day, Xu again posted the following content on his Sina Weibo (accompanied by nine photographs): “(I am also under various pressures; please understand, netizens.) The parents are from a certain district in Nanjing. The boy was lawfully adopted at age 6. The abusive conduct was discovered by the school last year. Initially, it was thought to be an occasional situation, and not much was said. Recently, the boy's homeroom teacher found that the boy's injuries were becoming increasingly severe, and his personality had also changed significantly, showing psychological behavior such as fear of crowds. After multiple efforts by the homeroom teacher and subject teachers to no avail, they attempted to seek help online. We earnestly request the assistance of the media and everyone.” Without permission, Xu published Shi's portrait publicly, against Shi's will. Xu's conduct infringed upon Shi's portrait rights. Without permission, Xu publicly disclosed information that Shi was an adopted child; Li (Shi's adoptive mother) did not abuse the child, but Xu, without any factual basis, claimed that Li had long abused Shi, causing Li to suffer unwarranted criticism from others, artificially harming the relationship between Shi and his adoptive mother. Xu's conduct seriously infringed upon Shi's right to privacy and right to a peaceful life. After Xu posted the matter of Li hitting Shi online under the label of child abuse, it attracted nationwide and sustained attention, making Shi known as a “bad child.” Xu's conduct seriously infringed upon Shi's right to reputation. Xu's conduct caused the family privacy and financial difficulties of Zhang and Gui to be ruthlessly exposed to the public, seriously infringing upon the privacy rights of Zhang and Gui. Xu's conduct caused Zhang and Gui to be unjustly labeled as having “abandoned” their child, leading relatives, friends, and the public to make negative evaluations of Zhang and Gui's decision to give their child up for adoption, seriously infringing upon the reputation rights of Zhang and Gui. They requested the court to order Xu to cease the infringement; to apologize and eliminate the effects and restore their reputation nationwide; to pay Shi RMB 100,000 in moral damages; and to pay Zhang and Gui RMB 100,000 in moral damages.

Defendant Xu argued: Shi is a minor. Under circumstances where he had suffered serious physical harm, Xu posted photographs of Shi's injuries to seek public help. Moreover, when posting the photographs, he applied a mosaic effect to Shi's face to the extent that it did not affect the facts. His purpose was to promptly prevent further domestic violence and to protect the minor, not for profit. Although he used Shi's portrait without Shi's consent, it fell within the circumstances permitted by law, and therefore he did not infringe Shi's portrait rights. The information that Shi was an adopted child becomes part of the public domain upon lawful adoption; Shi's claim that this information is his private information improperly expands the scope of privacy. The reference to the adoption relationship was intended to protect the minor from further harm, hoping that the civil affairs department would review the adoption relationship and take action. His conduct did not infringe privacy rights. The content of his Weibo post was merely a statement of the facts. After investigation by the public security authorities, it was confirmed to be completely true, and the perpetrator was dealt with according to law. The Weibo post contained nothing that would lower Shi's social evaluation or create an image of a “bad child” who lies or does not like to study, etc. It did not harm Shi's reputation and did not constitute infringement. The content of his Weibo post did not involve any information about Zhang or Gui. Zhang and Gui's claim that he had infringed their privacy and reputation rights was entirely without factual or legal basis. He requested the court to dismiss all claims of the three plaintiffs.

The court of first instance, the Jiangning District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, found the following facts:

Plaintiffs Zhang and Gui are the biological parents of Plaintiff Shi. Li is Zhang's cousin. On June 3, 2013, after adoption registration by the Lai'an County Civil Affairs Bureau of Anhui Province, Shi was adopted by Li and Shi (the adoptive father). On April 5, 2015, the public security organs criminally detained Li on suspicion of intentional injury, which was later changed to bail pending investigation. The Pukou District People's Procuratorate of Nanjing initiated a public prosecution against Li for suspected intentional injury, and the case was pending trial. On April 5, 2015, Shi was placed under the temporary guardianship of his biological parents, Zhang and Gui, by the relevant government departments.

On May 5, 2015, the Nanjing Public Security Bureau Material Evidence Appraisal Center issued a Material Evidence Examination Report, concluding that the two seals affixed to the “Certificate of No Children for the Adopting Parties” submitted by Li and Shi when handling the adoption registration were inconsistent with the genuine seals. Li, when questioned by the public security authorities, stated that Shi's injuries were caused by her.

On April 3, 2015, at 21:15, Xu posted the following content (accompanied by nine photographs of Plaintiff Shi's injuries) on his Sina Weibo account (username “朝廷半日闲”): “The parents are from a certain district in Nanjing. The boy was lawfully adopted at age 6. The abusive conduct was discovered by the school last year. Recently, the homeroom teacher found that the injuries were becoming increasingly severe, and the child's personality had also changed significantly, showing psychological behavior such as fear of crowds. After multiple efforts by the homeroom teacher and subject teachers to no avail, they sought help online. We earnestly request the assistance of the media and everyone. We hope that through our help, this child can escape his current predicament.” He later deleted this post.

At 22:40 on the same day, Defendant Xu again posted the following content (accompanied by nine photographs of Plaintiff Shi's injuries) on his Sina Weibo (username “朝廷半日闲”): “(I am also under various pressures; please understand, netizens.) The parents are from a certain district in Nanjing. The boy was lawfully adopted at age 6. The abusive conduct was discovered by the school last year. Initially, it was thought to be an occasional situation, and not much was said. Recently, the boy's homeroom teacher found that the boy's injuries were becoming increasingly severe, and his personality had also changed significantly, showing psychological behavior such as fear of crowds. After multiple efforts by the homeroom teacher and subject teachers to no avail, they attempted to seek help online. We earnestly request the assistance of the media and everyone.” This Weibo post was deleted by Xu before May 8, 2015.

Among the same set of nine photographs uploaded twice by Defendant Xu on his Sina Weibo, three depicted the head and face of a person. On both uploads, the head and face were blurred, and the nine photographs no longer had clear identifiability.

Thereafter, the Sina Weibo post published by Defendant Xu was repeatedly reported on the internet and in the media.

The Jiangning District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province held at first instance:

A party has the responsibility to provide evidence for its claims. A person who causes damage to another's civil rights and interests through fault shall bear tort liability. If the damage is caused by a third party, the third party shall bear tort liability.

Regarding whether Defendant Xu infringed Plaintiff Shi's portrait rights: Article 100 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC provides that citizens enjoy the right to their own likeness; the use of a citizen's likeness for profit without the consent of the person concerned is prohibited. Article 6, paragraph 2, of the Law of the PRC on the Protection of Minors provides that any organization or individual has the right to dissuade, stop, or report to the relevant departments any conduct that infringes upon the lawful rights and interests of minors. In this case, after learning that Shi had been harmed, Xu used nine photographs of Shi's injuries for the purpose of exposing possible criminal conduct and protecting the minor's lawful rights and interests. Although this was done without Shi's consent, the use was to safeguard the social public interest and Shi's own interests, was not for profit, and the faces in the photographs were already blurred when used. Therefore, it should be determined that this use did not constitute an infringement of Shi's portrait rights.

Regarding whether Defendant Xu infringed the reputation rights of Plaintiffs Shi, Zhang, and Gui: Article 101 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC provides that citizens and legal persons enjoy the right to reputation. The dignity of citizens is protected by law. It is prohibited to harm the reputation of citizens or legal persons by means such as insult or defamation. Publicizing another person's privacy in writing or orally, or fabricating facts to openly demean another person's personality, or harming another person's reputation through insult, defamation, or similar means, causing a certain impact, shall be deemed as an act infringing upon a citizen's right to reputation. In this case, Xu publicly disclosed the fact that a male child had been subjected to abuse through the internet. This was a form of public online reporting and did not involve subjective fault. The content of Xu's Weibo post neither exaggerated nor concealed the facts, nor did it fabricate, spread rumors, or slander. The injuries suffered by Shi objectively existed. The content of the Weibo post was substantially consistent with the objective facts. The Weibo post did not use insulting or defamatory language and would not objectively lower Shi's social prestige and evaluation. The content of Xu's Weibo post did not involve any information about Zhang or Gui, and there was no insult or defamation directed at Zhang or Gui. Shi, Zhang, and Gui also failed to provide sufficient evidence to prove that their reputation was damaged due to Xu's online posting. Therefore, the claims of Shi, Zhang, and Gui that Xu infringed their reputation rights were not established.

Regarding whether Defendant Xu infringed the privacy rights of Plaintiffs Shi, Zhang, and Gui: The right to privacy is a personality right enjoyed by a natural person to control personal information, private activities, and private domains that are unrelated to the public interest. Whether an infringement of the right to privacy has occurred shall be determined based on the existence of actual damage to the victim's privacy, the illegality of the actor's conduct, a causal relationship between the illegal conduct and the damage, and the actor's subjective fault. In this case, Xu was restrained in disclosing the relevant information. He blurred the relevant photographs, did not expose the real facial features of the victim child, and did not disclose Shi's name or home address. His purpose was to expose possible criminal conduct. Although the content of Xu's Weibo post included the word “adoption,” when combining the text and photographs, a third party could not clearly identify that the victim child in the Weibo post was Shi. The content of Xu's Weibo post did not involve any information about Zhang or Gui. As for the fact that after Xu posted the Weibo, netizens searched for Zhang and Gui, leading to the disclosure of their relevant information, Xu should not be held responsible for that. Therefore, the claims of Shi, Zhang, and Gui that Xu infringed their privacy rights were not established.

In summary, after Plaintiff Shi was injured, Defendant Xu published information about the minor's injuries on his Weibo for the purpose of protecting the minor's interests and exposing possible criminal conduct. This was in compliance with the principle of social public interest and the principle of the best interests of the child. Xu's online reporting did not infringe upon Shi's portrait rights, reputation rights, or privacy rights, nor did it infringe upon the reputation rights or privacy rights of Plaintiffs Zhang and Gui. The claims of Shi, Zhang, and Gui were without legal basis and were not supported.

Accordingly, in accordance with Articles 100 and 101 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, Articles 2, 6(1), and 28 of the Tort Liability Law of the PRC, Article 6(2) of the Law of the PRC on the Protection of Minors, and Articles 39, 64, and 134 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the Jiangning District People's Court of Nanjing, Jiangsu Province rendered the following judgment on September 25, 2015:

All claims of Plaintiffs Shi, Zhang, and Gui were dismissed.

After the judgment of first instance, neither the plaintiffs nor the defendant appealed, and the judgment has become legally effective.
